Actinium is a radioactive chemical element with symbol Ac (not to be confused with the abbreviation for an acetyl group) and atomic number 89, which was discovered in 1899. It was the first non-primordial radioactive element to be isolated. Polonium, radium and radon were observed before actinium, but they were not isolated until 1902.

Actinium is so radioactive that a sample can ionize surrounding air and appear to glow blue. It begins the actinide series and occurs only in traces in uranium ores. Actinium-225 is now prized for targeted therapies that deliver powerful alpha radiation over cellular distances.
Adding it to mercury-vapour lamps produces artificial light that closely mimics natural sunlight.
Adding it to steel helps make durable tools and vehicle parts.

Alkali metals occupy group 1, below hydrogen. Their outer electron is comparatively easy to remove, and their compounds are commonly described using a +1 oxidation state. The familiar members are soft, reactive metals that are normally encountered in compounds rather than as uncombined metal in nature. Reactivity, melting point, and other properties change as the atoms become larger down the group.

Alkaline earth metals form group 2. Their two outer electrons help explain why +2 is their characteristic oxidation state in compounds. Compared with the neighboring alkali metals, they generally bind their electrons more strongly and are harder and less reactive. The group includes elements important in rocks, biological structures, and alloys, but its members differ considerably in solubility, chemical behavior, and biological effects.

Aluminium (or aluminum; see different endings) is a chemical element in the boron group with symbol Al and atomic number 13. It is a silvery-white, soft, nonmagnetic, ductile metal. Aluminium is the third most abundant element (after oxygen and silicon), and the most abundant metal, in the Earth's crust.

Aluminum is common in Earth’s crust but binds oxygen so tightly that extracting the metal requires substantial electricity. Once exposed to air, it forms an ultrathin oxide skin that protects the surface below. That self-protection helps explain its success in aircraft, cans, wiring, and architecture.

Americium is a radioactive transuranic chemical element with symbol Am and atomic number 95. This member of the actinide series is located in the periodic table under the lanthanide element europium, and thus by analogy was named after the Americas. Americium was first produced in 1944 by the group of Glenn T.Seaborg from Berkeley, California, at the metallurgical laboratory of University of Chicago.

Americium-241 emits alpha particles that ionize air inside many smoke detectors. Smoke disrupts the tiny current, triggering the alarm. The element was created during wartime plutonium research, then named for the Americas by analogy with europium across the lanthanide row.

Antimony compounds darkened eyes in ancient cosmetics and later hardened lead for type, batteries, and ammunition. Today much of the element goes into materials designed to slow ignition. Antimony is a metalloid: its brittle, silvery appearance is metallic, but its electrical behavior is more complicated.

Antimony is a chemical element with symbol Sb (from Latin:stibium) and atomic number 51. A lustrous gray metalloid, it is found in nature mainly as the sulfide mineral stibnite (Sb2S3). Antimony compounds have been known since ancient times and were used for cosmetics; metallic antimony was also known, but it was erroneously identified as lead upon its discovery.

Argon is a chemical element with symbol Ar and atomic number 18. It is in group 18 of the periodic table and is a noble gas. Argon is the third most common gas in the Earth's atmosphere, at 0.934% (9,340 ppmv), making it over twice as abundant as the next most common atmospheric gas, water vapor (which averages about 4000 ppmv, but varies greatly), and 23 times as abundant as the next most common non-condensing atmospheric gas, carbon dioxide (400 ppmv), and more than 500 times as abundant as the next most common noble gas, neon (18 ppmv).

Argon makes up almost one percent of the atmosphere, more than carbon dioxide, yet it went unrecognized because it reacts so little. Its chemical quietness creates protective atmospheres for welding, metal production, and sensitive experiments. In lamps, electrical excitation gives argon a violet-blue glow.

Arsenic is a chemical element with symbol As and atomic number 33. Arsenic occurs in many minerals, usually in conjunction with sulfur and metals, and also as a pure elemental crystal. Arsenic is a metalloid.

Arsenic is infamous as a poison, but its story also includes pigments, medicines, semiconductors, and natural groundwater contamination. Different chemical forms vary greatly in toxicity. Gallium arsenide, for example, is a crystalline electronic material whose behavior bears little resemblance to elemental arsenic.
As an ion, it is essential for transmitting nerve impulses throughout the body.

Astatine appears fleetingly in natural radioactive decay chains; at any moment Earth’s crust probably contains far less than a kilogram. No one has assembled enough to see a bulk sample. Its chemistry is inferred from tracer experiments, and selected isotopes are studied for targeted alpha-particle cancer therapy.

At any given moment, fewer than 30 grams of it are estimated to exist in the entire Earth's crust.

Atomic clocks built using this element are among the most precise timekeeping devices ever constructed.

Barium is a chemical element with symbol Ba and atomic number 56. It is the fifth element in Group 2, a soft silvery metallic alkaline earth metal. Because of its high chemical reactivity barium is never found in nature as a free element.

Barium metal is dangerously reactive, but insoluble barium sulfate can pass through the body with little absorption. Its opacity to X-rays outlines the digestive system during medical imaging. Other barium compounds color fireworks green and help drilling fluids counter pressure deep underground.

Before its dangers were understood, it was added to health tonics and drinking water as a supposed miraculous cure-all.
Below 13 °C it slowly crumbles from a shiny metal into a grey powder, a phenomenon historically called "tin pest."

Berkelium is a transuranic radioactive chemical element with symbol Bk and atomic number 97. It is a member of the actinide and transuranium element series. It is named after the city of Berkeley, California, the location of the University of California Radiation Laboratory where it was discovered in December 1949.

Berkelium was first produced at the University of California, Berkeley, continuing a geographic naming chain that includes terbium and californium. It exists only in tiny manufactured quantities. Even so, a carefully prepared berkelium target enabled the creation of tennessine decades later.

Beryllium combines low mass with remarkable stiffness, so small amounts strengthen aerospace structures and precision instruments. It barely absorbs X-rays, making thin beryllium windows useful in detectors. The same element demands strict handling, because inhaled beryllium dust can cause serious chronic lung disease.

Beryllium is a chemical element with symbol Be and atomic number 4. It is created through stellar nucleosynthesis and is a relatively rare element in the universe. It is a divalent element which occurs naturally only in combination with other elements in minerals.

Bismuth crystals grow stepped shapes and acquire iridescent oxide films that create their familiar rainbow colors. The element is far less toxic than neighboring lead and appears in medicines and low-melting alloys. Bismuth-209 is radioactive, but its half-life is vastly longer than the age of the universe.

Bismuth is a chemical element with symbol Bi and atomic number 83. Bismuth, a pentavalent post-transition metal, chemically resembles arsenic and antimony. Elemental bismuth may occur naturally, although its sulfide and oxide form important commercial ores.

Bohrium honors Niels Bohr, whose atomic model helped make sense of periodic behavior. Its atoms are produced in heavy-ion collisions and usually decay within seconds. Chemists have nevertheless formed a volatile bohrium compound, finding behavior consistent with heavier-member status beneath rhenium.

Bohrium is a chemical element with symbol Bh and atomic number 107. It is named after Danish physicist Niels Bohr. It is a synthetic element (an element that can be created in a laboratory but is not found in nature) and radioactive; the most stable known isotope, 270Bh, has a half-life of approximately 61 seconds.

Boron is a metalloid chemical element with symbol B and atomic number 5. Produced entirely by cosmic ray spallation and supernovae and not by stellar nucleosynthesis, it is a low-abundance element in both the Solar system and the Earth's crust. Boron is concentrated on Earth by the water-solubility of its more common naturally occurring compounds, the borate minerals.

Boron sits between metallic and nonmetallic behavior. Its strong covalent networks help borosilicate glass survive sudden temperature changes, while boron carbide ranks among the hardest known materials. The isotope boron-10 captures neutrons so readily that it is used to help control nuclear reactions.
Brazil nuts are extraordinarily rich in it — just one nut can exceed the recommended daily intake.

Bromine (from Ancient Greek:βρῶμος, brómos, meaning "stench") is a chemical element with symbol Br, and atomic number 35. It is a halogen. The element was isolated independently by two chemists, Carl Jacob Löwig and Antoine Jerome Balard, in 1825–1826.

Bromine is a fuming red-brown liquid at room temperature, its molecules volatile enough to fill the space above it with corrosive vapor. Bromide compounds occur throughout seawater. Photography, flame retardants, drilling fluids, and medicines have all drawn on bromine chemistry, sometimes with environmental costs.

Cadmium is a chemical element with symbol Cd and atomic number 48. This soft, bluish-white metal is chemically similar to the two other stable metals in group 12, zinc and mercury. Like zinc, it prefers oxidation state +2 in most of its compounds and like mercury it shows a low melting point compared to transition metals.

Cadmium’s corrosion resistance once encouraged widespread electroplating, pigments, and rechargeable batteries. The element accumulates in kidneys and can weaken bone, leading to tighter controls and recycling programs. Cadmium telluride solar cells remain an important modern use, sealed into thin semiconductor layers.

Caesium or cesium is a chemical element with symbol Cs and atomic number 55. It is a soft, silvery-gold alkali metal with a melting point of 28 °C (82 °F), which makes it one of only five elemental metals that are liquid at or near room temperature. Caesium is an alkali metal and has physical and chemical properties similar to those of rubidium and potassium.

Calcium gives structure to shells, teeth, and skeletons, mostly through mineral compounds rather than pure metal. Cells also use tiny bursts of calcium ions as internal messages that trigger muscle contraction and many other processes. Limestone, cement, gypsum, and plaster extend calcium’s influence into cities.

Calcium is a chemical element with symbol Ca and atomic number 20. Calcium is a soft gray alkaline earth metal, fifth-most-abundant element by mass in the Earth's crust. The ion Ca2+ is also the fifth-most-abundant dissolved ion in seawater by both molarity and mass, after sodium, chloride, magnesium, and sulfate.

Californium is a radioactive metallic chemical element with symbol Cf and atomic number 98. The element was first made in 1950 at the University of California Radiation Laboratory in Berkeley, by bombarding curium with alpha particles (helium-4 ions). It is an actinide element, the sixth transuranium element to be synthesized, and has the second-highest atomic mass of all the elements that have been produced in amounts large enough to see with the unaided eye (after einsteinium).

Californium-252 undergoes spontaneous fission often enough to act as an intense compact neutron source. It can start reactors, inspect materials, and help analyze ores. That usefulness comes with formidable shielding, security, scarcity, and cost: annual production is measured in very small amounts.
Can be used to make strong permanent magnets.
Can form materials that are either very hard or soft and flaky.

Carbon (from Latin:carbo "coal") is a chemical element with symbol C and atomic number 6. On the periodic table, it is the first (row 2) of six elements in column (group) 14, which have in common the composition of their outer electron shell. It is nonmetallic and tetravalent—making four electrons available to form covalent chemical bonds.

Cerium is a chemical element with symbol Ce and atomic number 58. It is a soft, silvery, ductile metal which easily oxidizes in air. Cerium was named after the dwarf planet Ceres (itself named after the Roman goddess of agriculture).

Cerium is the most abundant lanthanide. It switches readily between two oxidation states, allowing cerium oxide to store and release oxygen in catalytic converters. Mischmetal rich in cerium makes lighter flints; scraping it creates hot sparks rather than merely exposing a glowing ember.

Chlorine gas is corrosive and dangerous, yet dilute chlorine chemistry transformed public health by controlling microbes in drinking water. Chloride—the element after gaining an electron—is far less aggressive and is essential in body fluids and table salt. The difference illustrates how dramatically chemical form changes risk.

Chlorine is a chemical element with symbol Cl and atomic number 17. It also has a relative atomic mass of 35.5. Chlorine is in the halogen group (17) and is the second lightest halogen following fluorine.

Chromium gives stainless steel its defining resistance to rust. Oxygen creates a transparent chromium-rich film that seals scratches almost as soon as they appear. Chromium compounds also span vivid pigments and industrial hazards: the trivalent form is far less dangerous than strongly oxidizing hexavalent chromium.

Chromium is a chemical element with symbol Cr and atomic number 24. It is the first element in Group 6. It is a steely-gray, lustrous, hard and brittle metal which takes a high polish, resists tarnishing, and has a high melting point.

Cobalt compounds have colored ceramics blue for centuries, long before the metal was understood. Today cobalt appears in heat-resistant superalloys, rechargeable batteries, and strong magnets. Biology needs only traces—vitamin B12 contains a cobalt atom—while excessive exposure is harmful.

Cobalt is a chemical element with symbol Co and atomic number 27. Like nickel, cobalt in the Earth's crust is found only in chemically combined form, save for small deposits found in alloys of natural meteoric iron. The free element, produced by reductive smelting, is a hard, lustrous, silver-gray metal.

Copernicium is a chemical element with symbol Cn and atomic number 112. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element that can only be created in a laboratory. The most stable known isotope, copernicium-285, has a half-life of approximately 29 seconds, but it is possible that this copernicium isotope may have a nuclear isomer with a longer half-life, 8.9 min.

Copernicium is named for Nicolaus Copernicus and occupies the position below mercury. Its electrons move so rapidly that relativistic effects strongly reshape its predicted chemistry. Experiments suggest surprising volatility, fueling debate over how metallic a bulk sample would be—if one could exist.

Copper carries electricity efficiently while remaining ductile enough to draw into long wires. Exposure gradually creates protective green and brown surface compounds, as seen on old roofs and statues. Long before electrical grids, copper and its alloy bronze helped define entire eras of tools and art.

Copper is a chemical element with symbol Cu (from Latin:cuprum) and atomic number 29. It is a soft, malleable and ductile metal with very high thermal and electrical conductivity. A freshly exposed surface of pure copper has a reddish-orange color.

Curium honors Marie and Pierre Curie, whose work transformed the study of radioactivity. It is made by bombarding lighter actinides with neutrons or charged particles and generates substantial heat as it decays. Curium sources have helped instruments on Mars analyze rocks by X-ray spectroscopy.

Curium is a transuranic radioactive chemical element with symbol Cm and atomic number 96. This element of the actinide series was named after Marie and Pierre Curie – both were known for their research on radioactivity. Curium was first intentionally produced and identified in July 1944 by the group of Glenn T. Seaborg at the University of California, Berkeley.

Darmstadtium is a chemical element with symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. The most stable known isotope, darmstadtium-281, has a half-life of approximately 10 seconds.

Darmstadtium was created at the GSI laboratory in Darmstadt by fusing nickel and lead nuclei. The experiment identified only a handful of decay chains, yet that evidence was enough to establish element 110. Predictions place it below platinum, modified by strong relativistic effects.
Despite being a solid metalloid, it is actually rarer in the Earth's crust than gold.
Despite being classified as a noble gas, it is predicted to be a solid at room temperature and potentially highly reactive.
Despite being lightweight, it is stiffer than steel.
Despite its fame in signs, it was only discovered on Earth in 1898.

Diamond, graphite, graphene, soot, and charcoal are all forms of carbon, distinguished by how their atoms connect. Carbon’s four bonding sites support chains, rings, sheets, and three-dimensional frameworks. That versatility is why carbon chemistry can describe both living cells and advanced engineered materials.

Dubnium atoms live just long enough for automated equipment to compare their behavior with niobium and tantalum. Laboratories at Dubna and Berkeley contested the discovery, producing a naming dispute settled only years later. The final name honors Dubna, the Russian nuclear-research center.

Dubnium is a chemical element with symbol Db and atomic number 105. It is named after the town of Dubna in Russia (north of Moscow), where it was first produced. It is a synthetic element (an element that can be created in a laboratory but is not found in nature) and radioactive; the most stable known isotope, dubnium-268, has a half-life of approximately 28 hours.

Dysprosium has a very large magnetic moment. Adding it to neodymium magnets helps them resist demagnetization at high operating temperatures, an advantage in compact motors and generators. The trade-off is supply: dysprosium is scarce, difficult to separate, and a target for recycling and material-saving designs.

Dysprosium is a chemical element with the symbol Dy and atomic number 66. It is a rare earth element with a metallic silver luster. Dysprosium is never found in nature as a free element, though it is found in various minerals, such as xenotime.

Einsteinium is a synthetic element with symbol Es and atomic number 99. It is the seventh transuranic element, and an actinide. Einsteinium was discovered as a component of the debris of the first hydrogen bomb explosion in 1952, and named after Albert Einstein.

Einsteinium was identified in debris from the 1952 Ivy Mike thermonuclear test. Its discovery was initially classified, and only minuscule quantities have ever been isolated. Intense self-irradiation damages samples and produces heat, complicating attempts to measure what ordinary einsteinium chemistry would look like.

Erbium ions can absorb pump-laser energy and release it at wavelengths used in fiber-optic communication. Erbium-doped amplifiers boost signals directly as light, avoiding repeated electrical conversion across oceans. The same ions give glass and crystals a characteristic delicate pink color.

Erbium is a chemical element in the lanthanide series, with symbol Er and atomic number 68. A silvery-white solid metal when artificially isolated, natural erbium is always found in chemical combination with other elements on Earth. As such, it is a rare earth element which is associated with several other rare elements in the mineral gadolinite from Ytterby in Sweden, where yttrium, ytterbium, and terbium were discovered.

Europium ions emit intense, sharply defined red and blue light when excited. Red phosphors made color television convincing, and modern security inks use the same optical fingerprints. Europium is also unusually willing among lanthanides to form a +2 ion, giving its chemistry a distinctive branch.

Europium is a chemical element with symbol Eu and atomic number 63. It was isolated in 1901 and is named after the continent of Europe. It is a moderately hard, silvery metal which readily oxidizes in air and water.

Flerovium honors the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions. It lies below lead, yet relativistic stabilization of its electrons may make it unusually volatile and weakly reactive for a metal. Experiments are difficult to interpret because each atom survives only briefly before radioactive decay.

Flerovium is a superheavy artificial chemical element with symbol Fl and atomic number 114. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. The element is named after the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia, where the element was discovered in 1998.
Flow batteries using this element are a leading technology for large-scale electricity grid storage.

Fluorine is a chemical element with symbol F and atomic number 9. It is the lightest halogen and exists as a highly toxic pale yellow diatomic gas at standard conditions. As the most electronegative element, it is extremely reactive:almost all other elements, including some noble gases, form compounds with fluorine.

Fluorine pulls on shared electrons more strongly than any other element. Lanthanum is soft, reactive, and usually found mixed with chemically similar lanthanides. Its compounds improve optical glass and serve in catalysts, while lanthanum-nickel alloys can store hydrogen. The name means “to lie hidden,” fitting an element concealed within a supposedly known mineral.

Lawrencium is traditionally placed at the end of the actinide row and named for cyclotron inventor Ernest Lawrence. Measurements of its outer electron challenge a simple extrapolation from lighter elements. That makes lawrencium central to debates over exactly where the next transition series begins.

Lead is dense, easy to shape, and effective at absorbing radiation and vibration. Those conveniences put it into pipes, paints, fuel, batteries, and buildings for centuries. Because the body mistakes lead for useful metals, even modest exposure can disrupt brain development; there is no known safe level for children.

Meitnerium is a chemical element with symbol Mt and atomic number 109. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element (an element not found in nature that can be created in a laboratory). The most stable known isotope, meitnerium-278, has a half-life of 7.6 seconds.

Mendelevium is a synthetic element with chemical symbol Md (formerly Mv) and atomic number 101. A metallic radioactive transuranic element in the actinide series, it is the first element that currently cannot be produced in macroscopic quantities through neutron bombardment of lighter elements. It is the antepenultimate actinide and the ninth transuranic element.

Mercury is a chemical element with symbol Hg and atomic number 80. It is commonly known as quicksilver and was formerly named hydrargyrum (/haɪˈdrɑːrdʒərəm/). A heavy, silvery d-block element, mercury is the only metallic element that is liquid at standard conditions for temperature and pressure; the only other element that is liquid under these conditions is bromine, though metals such as caesium, gallium, and rubidium melt just above room temperature.

Mercury is liquid at room temperature because its electrons bind the atoms together less effectively than expected for a heavy metal. That mobility made precise thermometers and barometers possible, but mercury vapor and methylmercury attack the nervous system. Modern controls reflect a hard-earned toxicological history.

Metalloids lie near the boundary between metals and nonmetals. The label describes a useful collection of intermediate properties rather than a single formal vertical group. Some have electrical behavior that can be tuned by adding small amounts of other elements, making them important in semiconductor materials. Their chemistry often involves covalent bonding, and the properties of their compounds can differ greatly from those of the pure elements.

Neodymium is a chemical element with symbol Nd and atomic number 60. It is a soft silvery metal that tarnishes in air. Neodymium was discovered in 1885 by the Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach.

Neodymium-iron-boron magnets pack extraordinary magnetic strength into small volumes. They sit inside headphones, hard drives, wind turbines, and electric-vehicle motors. Pure neodymium tarnishes quickly, so the useful magnet is a carefully engineered alloy with coatings that protect it from corrosion.

Neon is a chemical element with symbol Ne and atomic number 10. It is in group 18 (noble gases) of the periodic table. Neon is a colorless, odorless, inert monatomic gas under standard conditions, with about two-thirds the density of air.

Neptunium became the first transuranium element created by humans, extending the table beyond what was then considered its natural end. Reactors produce it from uranium. Neptunium-237 lasts long enough to matter in nuclear waste and can serve as feedstock for producing plutonium-238.

Neptunium is a chemical element with symbol Np and atomic number 93. A radioactive actinide metal, neptunium is the first transuranic element. Its position in the periodic table just after uranium, named after the planet Uranus, led to it being named after Neptune, the next planet beyond Uranus.

Nickel is a chemical element with symbol Ni and atomic number 28. It is a silvery-white lustrous metal with a slight golden tinge. Nickel belongs to the transition metals and is hard and ductile.

Nickel resists corrosion, mixes readily into alloys, and remains magnetic near room temperature. Stainless steel consumes much of the world’s supply. Earth’s accessible crust holds relatively little because vast amounts sank into the core; some metallic meteorites offer a glimpse of similar iron-nickel material.

Nihonium is a chemical element with atomic number 113. It has a symbol Nh. It is a synthetic element (an element that can be created in a laboratory but is not found in nature) and is extremely radioactive; its most stable known isotope, nihonium-286, has a half-life of 20 seconds.

Nihonium was the first element credited to a team in Asia. Researchers at RIKEN painstakingly linked a few atoms through characteristic decay chains before recognition was secured. Nihon is one Japanese name for Japan, so the element’s name records both place and scientific milestone.

Niobium strengthens steel in tiny additions and becomes superconducting at low temperature. Niobium-titanium wire forms the magnets in many MRI machines and particle accelerators. Its name emerged from a long confusion with tantalum—chemically similar neighbors whose mythological names are related.

Niobium, formerly columbium, is a chemical element with symbol Nb (formerly Cb) and atomic number 41. It is a soft, grey, ductile transition metal, which is often found in the pyrochlore mineral, the main commercial source for niobium, and columbite. The name comes from Greek mythology:Niobe, daughter of Tantalus since it is so similar to tantalum.

Nitrogen is a chemical element with symbol N and atomic number 7. It is the lightest pnictogen and at room temperature, it is a transparent, odorless diatomic gas. Nitrogen is a common element in the universe, estimated at about seventh in total abundance in the Milky Way and the Solar System.

Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol No and atomic number 102. It is named in honor of Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite and benefactor of science. A radioactive metal, it is the tenth transuranic element and is the penultimate member of the actinide series.

Nobelium’s history involved competing claims from laboratories in Sweden, the United States, and the Soviet Union. Later work resolved which experiments were convincing, while the name honoring Alfred Nobel survived. Its short-lived atoms reveal chemistry mainly through rapid automated separations.
Non-toxic metal with a beautiful rainbow-colored surface.

Unlike most metals, they are generally poor electrical conductors, although graphite is a notable exception. Several nonmetals are central to the chemistry of living organisms, air, water, and minerals.

Ordinary white tin is a workable metal used in solder and protective coatings. At low temperatures it can slowly convert into crumbly gray tin, a transformation nicknamed tin pest. Alloying usually suppresses the change, while tin plating protects steel food cans from corrosion.

Osmium (from Greek osme (ὀσμή) meaning "smell") is a chemical element with symbol Os and atomic number 76. It is a hard, brittle, bluish-white transition metal in the platinum group that is found as a trace element in alloys, mostly in platinum ores. Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, with a density of 22.59 g/cm3.

Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, narrowly competing with iridium depending on how density is calculated. The metal is hard and durable, but osmium tetroxide is volatile, intensely toxic, and pungent. Carefully controlled, that compound stains biological membranes for electron microscopy.

Oxygen is a chemical element with symbol O and atomic number 8. It is a member of the chalcogen group on the periodic table and is a highly reactive nonmetal and oxidizing agent that readily forms compounds (notably oxides) with most elements. By mass, oxygen is the third-most abundant element in the universe, after hydrogen and helium.

Oxygen’s appetite for electrons makes combustion possible and lets cells release energy from food. Photosynthetic organisms continually replenish atmospheric oxygen, but the element also dominates Earth’s crust by mass inside silicate minerals and oxides. Its pale-blue liquid form is visibly drawn toward a strong magnet.

Pairs of nitrogen atoms fill most of the atmosphere, held together by a stubborn triple bond. Life cannot use that reservoir directly, so microbes, lightning, and industry must “fix” nitrogen into reactive compounds. Those compounds feed crops, build proteins, and can also become powerful explosives.

Palladium can absorb an extraordinary amount of hydrogen into gaps within its crystal lattice. It is also a versatile catalyst, accelerating hydrogenation and carbon-carbon bond formation. Jewelry uses its pale, corrosion-resistant surface, while vehicle exhaust systems consume much of the available supply.

Palladium is a chemical element with symbol Pd and atomic number 46. It is a rare and lustrous silvery-white metal discovered in 1803 by William Hyde Wollaston. He named it after the asteroid Pallas, which was itself named after the epithet of the Greek goddess Athena, acquired by her when she slew Pallas.

Phosphorus atoms sit in DNA’s backbone and in ATP, the molecule cells use to move energy around. White phosphorus glows faintly as it reacts with air and can ignite spontaneously, whereas red phosphorus is far safer. Agriculture depends on phosphate fertilizers, but excess runoff can overwhelm waterways.

Phosphorus is a chemical element with symbol P and atomic number 15. As an element, phosphorus exists in two major forms—white phosphorus and red phosphorus—but due to its high reactivity, phosphorus is never found as a free element on Earth. Instead phosphorus-containing minerals are almost always present in their maximally oxidised state, as inorganic phosphate rocks.
Plants require enzymes containing this element to convert atmospheric nitrogen into a usable form.

Platinum is a chemical element with symbol Pt and atomic number 78. It is a dense, malleable, ductile, highly unreactive, precious, gray-white transition metal. Its name is derived from the Spanish term platina, which is literally translated into "little silver".

Platinum is dense, workable, and exceptionally resistant to corrosion. Its surface catalyzes reactions in exhaust systems, fuel cells, and chemical plants. Platinum compounds behave very differently from the metal: cisplatin damages DNA and became one of medicine’s most important chemotherapy drugs.

Plutonium is a transuranic radioactive chemical element with symbol Pu and atomic number 94. It is an actinide metal of silvery-gray appearance that tarnishes when exposed to air, and forms a dull coating when oxidized. The element normally exhibits six allotropes and four oxidation states.

Plutonium is famous for weapons and reactor fuel, but plutonium-238 has another identity. Its steady radioactive heat powers spacecraft traveling too far from the Sun for practical solar panels. Different isotopes have profoundly different nuclear roles, even though their chemistry is nearly identical.

Polonium is a chemical element with symbol Po and atomic number 84, discovered in 1898 by Marie Curie and Pierre Curie. A rare and highly radioactive element with no stable isotopes, polonium is chemically similar to bismuth and tellurium, and it occurs in uranium ores. Applications of polonium are few.

Potassium is a chemical element with symbol K (derived from Neo-Latin, kalium) and atomic number 19. It was first isolated from potash, the ashes of plants, from which its name is derived. In the Periodic table, potassium is one of seven elements in column (group) 1 (alkali metals):they all have a single valence electron in their outer electron shell, which they readily give up to create an atom with a positive charge - a cation, and combine with anions to form salts.

Potassium metal cannot be left in air or water, but potassium ions are indispensable inside cells. Carefully controlled flows of those ions help nerves signal and heart muscle reset between beats. Plants also require large amounts, which is why potassium compounds are a major component of fertilizer.

Praseodymium is a chemical element with symbol Pr and atomic number 59. Praseodymium is a soft, silvery, malleable and ductile metal in the lanthanide group. It is valued for its magnetic, electrical, chemical, and optical properties.

Promethium is the only lanthanide with no stable isotopes. Tiny natural traces arise from radioactive processes, but useful quantities are made in reactors. Its beta radiation has powered specialized long-life batteries and luminous devices, though scarcity and shielding requirements keep its applications narrow.

Promethium, originally prometheum, is a chemical element with the symbol Pm and atomic number 61. All of its isotopes are radioactive; it is one of only two such elements that are followed in the periodic table by elements with stable forms, a distinction shared with technetium. Chemically, promethium is a lanthanide, which forms salts when combined with other elements.

Protactinium is a chemical element with symbol Pa and atomic number 91. It is a dense, silvery-gray metal which readily reacts with oxygen, water vapor and inorganic acids. It forms various chemical compounds where protactinium is usually present in the oxidation state +5, but can also assume +4 and even +2 or +3 states.

Protactinium sits between uranium and actinium in a decay chain, which is exactly what its name announces. It is scarce, radioactive, and difficult to handle, so it has few uses outside research. Its complex electron behavior gives chemists a challenging bridge between lighter and heavier actinides.

Radium is a chemical element with symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It is the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table, also known as the alkaline earth metals. Pure radium is almost colorless, but it readily combines with nitrogen (rather than oxygen) on exposure to air, forming a black surface layer of radium nitride (Ra3N2).

Radium’s intense radioactivity once inspired luminous paints, patent medicines, and reckless health claims. Dial painters who ingested it exposed the lethal consequences and transformed workplace protections. Radium behaves like calcium, so the body can deposit it in bone, where radiation damages nearby tissue.

Radon forms when radium decays in rocks and soil. As a gas it can enter buildings through foundations, where inhaled decay products irradiate lung tissue. It has no smell or color, so testing—not human senses—is the only reliable way to find dangerous indoor accumulation.

Radon is a chemical element with symbol Rn and atomic number 86. It is a radioactive, colorless, odorless, tasteless noble gas, occurring naturally as a decay product of radium. Its most stable isotope, 222Rn, has a half-life of 3.8 days.

Rhenium is a chemical element with symbol Re and atomic number 75. It is a silvery-white, heavy, third-row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table. With an estimated average concentration of 1 part per billion (ppb), rhenium is one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust.

Rhenium is among the rarest elements in Earth’s crust. Added to nickel superalloys, it helps turbine blades resist creep inside the hottest parts of jet engines. Rhenium catalysts also reform petroleum molecules, while its extreme melting and boiling points reflect unusually strong metallic bonding.
Rhodium is a chemical element with symbol Rh and atomic number 45. It is a rare, silvery-white, hard, and chemically inert transition metal. It is a member of the platinum group.

Rhodium reflects light brilliantly and resists corrosion, but its greatest impact is less visible. Catalytic converters use it to reduce nitrogen oxides in exhaust. Because supply is tiny and tied to other platinum-group mining, rhodium prices can swing more dramatically than those of familiar precious metals.

Roentgenium honors Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays. It sits beneath gold in group 11, but no macroscopic sample exists to display a golden color or metallic surface. Calculations suggest relativistic electron behavior may give it properties unlike a straightforward heavier gold atom.

Roentgenium is a chemical element with symbol Rg and atomic number 111. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element (an element that can be created in a laboratory but is not found in nature); the most stable known isotope, roentgenium-282, has a half-life of 2.1 minutes. Roentgenium was first created in 1994 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research near Darmstadt, Germany.
Romans used it extensively in pipes and cooking vessels, and its Latin name is the origin of the word "plumbing."

Rubidium is a chemical element with symbol Rb and atomic number 37. Rubidium is a soft, silvery-white metallic element of the alkali metal group, with an atomic mass of 85.4678. Elemental rubidium is highly reactive, with properties similar to those of other alkali metals, such as very rapid oxidation in air.

Rubidium is a soft, reactive metal that must be protected from air. Its atoms respond to microwave frequencies with exceptional consistency, enabling compact atomic clocks used in telecommunications and navigation. Rubidium isotopes also help physicists cool gases toward quantum states where matter behaves collectively.

Ruthenium is a chemical element with symbol Ru and atomic number 44. It is a rare transition metal belonging to the platinum group of the periodic table. Like the other metals of the platinum group, ruthenium is inert to most other chemicals.

Ruthenium is a scarce, hard metal usually recovered while refining platinum ores. Minute additions can harden platinum and palladium, while ruthenium compounds catalyze useful chemical reactions. Its conductive oxides appear in electronic components, linking rare-metal refining to everyday circuitry.

Rutherfordium is a chemical element with symbol Rf and atomic number 104, named in honor of physicist Ernest Rutherford. It is a synthetic element (an element that can be created in a laboratory but is not found in nature) and radioactive; the most stable known isotope, 267Rf, has a half-life of approximately 1.3 hours. In the periodic table of the elements, it is a d - block element and the second of the fourth - row transition elements.

Rutherfordium opened the transactinide region, where atoms are created one at a time and vanish quickly. American and Soviet teams disputed priority and naming during the Cold War. Fast chemistry later showed that rutherfordium broadly resembles hafnium, as its position predicts.

Samarium is a chemical element with symbol Sm and atomic number 62. It is a moderately hard silvery metal that readily oxidizes in air. Being a typical member of the lanthanide series, samarium usually assumes the oxidation state +3.

Samarium-cobalt magnets retain strength at temperatures that weaken many neodymium magnets. That resilience suits aerospace, motors, and instruments exposed to heat. Samarium also absorbs neutrons effectively, while the isotope samarium-149 records part of the operating history of natural and engineered reactors.

Scandium is dispersed so thinly through minerals that concentrated ores are unusual. Small additions can make aluminum alloys stronger and easier to weld, useful where low mass matters. Scandium iodide in metal-halide lamps also helps produce light resembling natural daylight.

Selenium’s electrical conductivity increases under illumination, a response used in early photocopiers and light meters. Tiny amounts are nutritionally essential because selenium-containing enzymes protect cells. The safe range is narrow, however, and both deficiency and excess can cause harm.

Silicon is a chemical element with symbol Si and atomic number 14. It is a tetravalent metalloid, more reactive than germanium, the metalloid directly below it in the table. Controversy about silicon's character dates to its discovery.

Silicon links the mineral world to digital technology. In rocks it usually appears bonded to oxygen; in a purified crystal, tiny additions of other elements precisely tune its electrical behavior. Billions of microscopic silicon switches can therefore be patterned onto a chip and coordinated into a computer.

Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other element, though cost and tarnish keep copper dominant in ordinary wiring. Light-sensitive silver halides made film photography possible. Its ions can suppress microbes, a useful property that does not make indiscriminate “colloidal silver” remedies safe.

Silver is a chemical element with symbol Ag (Greek:άργυρος árguros, Latin:argentum, both from the Indo-European root *h₂erǵ- for "grey" or "shining") and atomic number 47. A soft, white, lustrous transition metal, it possesses the highest electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity and reflectivity of any metal. The metal occurs naturally in its pure, free form (native silver), as an alloy with gold and other metals, and in minerals such as argentite and chlorargyrite.
So little of it has ever been made that studying its basic chemical properties remains a significant scientific challenge.

Sodium /ˈsoʊdiəm/ is a chemical element with symbol Na (from Ancient Greek Νάτριο) and atomic number 11. It is a soft, silver-white, highly reactive metal. In the Periodic table it is in column 1 (alkali metals), and shares with the other six elements in that column that it has a single electron in its outer shell, which it readily donates, creating a positively charged atom - a cation.

Sodium metal is soft, silvery, and violently reactive with water; sodium ions are stable enough to circulate through blood and seawater. That contrast comes from losing a single outer electron. In the body, controlled sodium-ion movement creates the electrical pulses used by nerves and muscles.

Thorium is a chemical element with symbol Th and atomic number 90. A radioactive actinide metal, thorium is one of only two significantly radioactive elements that still occur naturally in large quantities as a primordial element (the other being uranium). It was discovered in 1828 by the Norwegian Reverend and amateur mineralogist Morten Thrane Esmark and identified by the Swedish chemist Jöns Jakob Berzelius, who named it after Thor, the Norse god of thunder.

Thorium-232 has a half-life comparable to the age of the universe, explaining why substantial deposits remain. It is fertile rather than directly fissile: reactors can convert it into uranium-233. Advocates see fuel-cycle advantages, although engineering, waste, economics, and proliferation questions remain.

Thulium is a chemical element with symbol Tm and atomic number 69. It is the thirteenth and antepenultimate (third-last) element in the lanthanide series. Like the other lanthanides, the most common oxidation state is +3, seen in its oxide, halides and other compounds.

Thulium is rare even among the rare earths, which limits large-scale uses. Its ions support lasers with medical and industrial wavelengths, while irradiated thulium can become a compact X-ray source. The metal’s scarcity makes such specialized applications more sensible than bulk ones.

Tin is a chemical element with the symbol Sn (for Latin:stannum) and atomic number 50. It is a main group metal in group 14 of the periodic table. Tin shows a chemical similarity to both neighboring group-14 elements, germanium and lead, and has two possible oxidation states, +2 and the slightly more stable +4.

Titanium has the strength expected of a heavy structural metal but a much lower density than steel. A tenacious oxide film protects it from corrosion, even in seawater and the body. Those traits connect jet-engine components, chemical equipment, artificial joints, and the brilliant white pigment titanium dioxide.

Titanium is a chemical element with symbol Ti and atomic number 22. It is a lustrous transition metal with a silver color, low density and high strength. It is highly resistant to corrosion in sea water, aqua regia and chlorine.

Tungsten has the highest melting point of any pure metal and remains strong at temperatures that soften most competitors. Those traits served incandescent filaments and now protect cutting tools, furnaces, and rocket hardware. Its symbol W preserves the older name wolfram.

Tungsten, also known as wolfram, is a chemical element with symbol W and atomic number 74. The word tungsten comes from the Swedish language tung sten, which directly translates to heavy stone. Its name in Swedish is volfram, however, in order to distinguish it from scheelite, which in Swedish is alternatively named tungsten.

Natural uranium also records geological time, colors some historic glass, and ultimately supplies the radon that can accumulate in buildings.

Xenon is a chemical element with symbol Xe and atomic number 54. It is a colorless, dense, odorless noble gas, that occurs in the Earth's atmosphere in trace amounts. Although generally unreactive, xenon can undergo a few chemical reactions such as the formation of xenon hexafluoroplatinate, the first noble gas compound to be synthesized.

Xenon’s heavy atoms are polarizable enough to form genuine compounds, overturning the old belief that noble gases were completely inert. It produces bright flashes in lamps, works as an anesthetic, and propels spacecraft in ion engines. Xenon is effective precisely because it is heavy and chemically clean.

Ytterbium is a chemical element with symbol Yb and atomic number 70. Yttrium is a chemical element with symbol Y and atomic number 39. It is a silvery-metallic transition metal chemically similar to the lanthanides and it has often been classified as a "rare earth element". Yttrium is almost always found combined with the lanthanides in rare earth minerals and is never found in nature as a free element.

Yttrium often travels with lanthanides in the same ores and behaves chemically like them, despite occupying a different position in the table. Yttrium compounds support red phosphors, lasers, superconductors, and tough ceramics. Its oxide also stabilizes zirconia used in dental crowns and oxygen sensors.

Zinc protects steel by corroding in its place, a process called galvanization. The body uses zinc ions in hundreds of proteins, including enzymes and DNA-binding structures. Brass combines zinc with copper, while zinc oxide lends ultraviolet protection to sunscreens and rubber products.

Zinc, in commerce also spelter, is a chemical element with symbol Zn and atomic number 30. It is the first element of group 12 of the periodic table. In some respects zinc is chemically similar to magnesium:its ion is of similar size and its only common oxidation state is +2.

Zirconium is a chemical element with symbol Zr and atomic number 40. The name of zirconium is taken from the name of the mineral zircon, the most important source of zirconium. The word zircon comes from the Persian word zargun زرگون, meaning "gold-colored".

Zirconium withstands aggressive chemicals and barely absorbs neutrons, a rare combination that suits nuclear-reactor fuel cladding. The metal must be separated meticulously from hafnium, which occurs beside it but captures neutrons strongly. Cubic zirconia is zirconium dioxide, not metallic zirconium.
